paragraphs: This paper studies constrained optimization when an algorithm can evaluate an objective but cannot directly access its gradients. It also avoids projection operations used to enforce constraints. The proposed methods combine these two properties within a zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe framework, targeting nonconvex objectives expressed either as finite sums or through stochastic observations.

The main method, Acc-SZOFW, combines SPIDER/SpiderBoost variance reduction with a new momentum acceleration technique. Under the stated mild conditions, it requires O(d√n ε⁻²) function queries for finite-sum problems and O(d ε⁻³) for stochastic problems to reach an ε-stationary point. Here, d represents dimension and n the finite-sum size. These guarantees concern approximate stationarity rather than finding a global optimum.

A second method, Acc-SZOFW*, uses STORM-based variance reduction to retain the stochastic query bound without large batches. The authors also generalize their momentum technique into an accelerated Frank-Wolfe framework. Experiments on black-box adversarial attacks and robust black-box classification support the efficiency of the proposed algorithms, connecting the query-complexity improvements to applications where gradient access is unavailable.
icml-2020-accelerated-stochastic-gradien.tldr: Accelerated Frank-Wolfe methods reduce function-query costs for constrained nonconvex optimization without gradients or projections.

paragraphs: Variational inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo are often presented as contrasting ways to approximate a posterior distribution: one optimizes a tractable approximation, while the other samples through a chain. This paper investigates a closer relationship between their gradient-based forms, focusing on how their errors evolve before either procedure has settled.

Analyzing the Fokker-Planck equation for Langevin dynamics, the authors show that its probability distribution follows a gradient flow corresponding to variational inference with a nonparametric normalizing flow. This connection suggests that bias from an incompletely run sampling chain may evolve similarly to bias from unfinished variational optimization. Differences from the variational parameterization and its eventual approximation bias still matter.

Experiments find similar evolution of these transient biases, including for momentum-accelerated versions. The practical implication is conditional: with limited computation time, an MCMC procedure might produce more accurate estimates even before burn-in is complete, provided its estimator variance can be controlled. Running many parallel chains is offered as one way to address that variance.
icml-2020-black-box-variational-inferenc.tldr: Langevin sampling and variational inference share a gradient-flow connection that helps explain their similar transient biases.

paragraphs: This paper considers finding a leading eigenvector when observations are distributed across multiple machines. This is a central problem in principal component analysis: identifying a dominant direction in the data. The computational challenge includes coordinating the machines, so the authors focus on reducing communication rather than only reducing local calculations.

Their algorithm uses Riemannian optimization and deliberately exchanges additional local computation for fewer global communications. The theoretical analysis establishes linear convergence, measured in communication rounds, to the centralized empirical risk minimization solution. In this usage, linear convergence means geometric error reduction across rounds. The target is the solution associated with the combined observed data.

The communication advantage has an explicit condition: each machine must hold sufficiently many data points. In that setting, the authors establish a significant reduction in communication cost relative to existing distributed PCA algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the communication benefit. The result therefore links a mathematical convergence guarantee with a practical tradeoff between computation performed locally and information exchanged globally.
icml-2020-communication-efficient-distri.tldr: A Riemannian optimization algorithm reduces distributed PCA communication by doing more local computation, with benefits when local datasets are sufficiently large.

paragraphs: Curvature-aware optimization adjusts learning updates to account for the shape of a loss landscape. Although these adjustments can accelerate training, their effects on the trajectory of network parameters are more complicated. This paper investigates those effects in deep linear neural networks, where the authors can derive analytical solutions for the learning dynamics.

A generalized conservation law shows that, in the analyzed setting, curvature correction preserves the path taken by the parameters while changing how quickly they move along it. This separates the geometry of the learning trajectory from its timing. The analysis also shows faster convergence of the network’s input-output map, alongside the possibility of worse generalization.

The authors identify another adverse effect: curvature correction can destabilize parameter dynamics, particularly when natural gradient descent uses a block-diagonal approximation. They introduce fractional curvature correction to resolve this stability problem while retaining most of the acceleration from full correction. The contribution explains why faster convergence, stable parameter evolution, and good generalization need to be considered separately within this analytical setting.
icml-2020-curvature-corrected-learning-d.tldr: Analysis of deep linear networks shows how curvature correction accelerates learning while potentially harming stability and generalization.

paragraphs: This paper explores speech recognition through relationships among utterances. Its motivation comes from relational thinking: new sensory information can be interpreted through connections to prior knowledge. Modeling this idea is difficult because the possible relational structures are numerous and the underlying relationships are not directly observed in the training data.

The proposed deep graph random process is a Bayesian nonparametric deep learning method that can generate infinitely many probabilistic graphs representing these possible relationships. The authors also derive a closed-form solution for combining and transforming the graphs for acoustic modeling. This gives the relational representation a defined computational role in the speech recognition model.

The method infers relationships among utterances without requiring relational training data. Evaluations on speech recognition tasks, including CHiME-2 and CHiME-5, demonstrate benefits from the approach. The stated contribution is therefore both representational and practical: it supplies a probabilistic way to model unobserved utterance relationships and shows that those inferred relationships can be useful for acoustic modeling.
icml-2020-deep-graph-random-process-for-.tldr: A Bayesian graph process infers unobserved relationships among utterances and uses them to improve acoustic modeling for speech recognition.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel provides a way to describe gradient-descent training in overparameterized networks. However, prediction using the limiting kernel can perform differently from an actual deep network. This paper studies finite-width learning dynamics to develop a richer mathematical description beyond that limiting kernel account.

The authors derive an infinite collection of linked differential equations called the neural tangent hierarchy. Successive levels provide higher-order extensions of the neural tangent kernel description. Truncating the hierarchy at level two recovers NTK dynamics, placing the familiar kernel model inside a broader family of descriptions rather than treating it as an isolated approximation.

The main approximation result is conditional on network width and dataset dimension. Under the required conditions, a hierarchy truncated at a level of at least two can approximate NTK dynamics to arbitrary precision. The assumptions become weaker as the truncation level increases. This establishes a controlled framework for studying finite-width effects and clarifies how adding higher-order dynamics can extend the reach of kernel-based analysis.
icml-2020-dynamics-of-deep-neural-networ.tldr: The neural tangent hierarchy extends NTK analysis with higher-order equations that approximate finite-width training dynamics under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Realistic-looking generated images or audio do not by themselves provide a complete quantitative evaluation of a generative model. Log-likelihood offers a statistical measure, but it can be difficult to estimate for implicit models and compresses quality into one number. This paper proposes evaluating models through their rate-distortion curves instead.

A rate-distortion curve describes the tradeoff between compression rate and reconstruction distortion. Examining that tradeoff exposes multiple operating points rather than reducing a model to a single score. Although estimating a whole curve appears expensive, the authors show that it can be approximated with nearly the same computations previously used for one log-likelihood estimate.

The study evaluates variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and adversarial autoencoders on MNIST and CIFAR10. The resulting curves reveal insights unavailable from log-likelihood alone. The contribution is therefore an evaluation approach that makes a richer compression-based comparison computationally accessible, helping characterize how models behave across different levels of tolerated information loss.
icml-2020-evaluating-lossy-compression-r.tldr: Rate-distortion curves provide a richer generative-model evaluation at nearly the computational cost of a single log-likelihood estimate.

paragraphs: CUR decomposition approximates a data matrix using selected columns and rows from the original matrix. Keeping those original components makes the approximation interpretable. In the deterministic approach studied here, selection is obtained by optimizing an objective with sparsity-inducing norms, but the coordinate-descent procedure can spend substantial time repeatedly updating parameters.

The paper accelerates this optimization by checking which updates are actually needed. It efficiently evaluates optimality conditions that identify parameters that should be zero, allowing unnecessary updates to be skipped safely. It also prioritizes updates to parameters that must be nonzero, directing computational effort toward components that matter to the solution.

The theoretical guarantee is that this change in update strategy preserves the result of the original approach. Experiments demonstrate faster deterministic CUR decomposition with the same accuracy. The value of the method is thus in making an existing interpretable approximation procedure cheaper to compute while retaining its solution guarantee, rather than obtaining speed through a less accurate decomposition.
icml-2020-fast-deterministic-cur-matrix-.tldr: Safe skipping and prioritization of coordinate updates accelerate deterministic CUR decomposition while preserving the original result.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods improve a policy using estimates of how its performance changes with its parameters. Off-policy evaluation addresses the related task of estimating policy performance from data. This paper connects the two by showing how policy-gradient estimators can be derived from importance-sampling-based estimators of policy value.

The construction takes finite differences of the value estimates. Through this perspective, the authors recover on-policy policy gradients and existing variance-reduction variants. Starting specifically from a doubly robust value estimator produces a flexible policy-gradient form that includes a leading variance-reduction technique as a special case and points toward additional opportunities to reduce variance.

The authors analyze the new estimator’s variance and compare it with existing methods and the Cramer-Rao lower bound for policy gradients. They also provide empirical evidence of effectiveness. The significance is a shared derivation that connects evaluation and optimization: improvements in how policy values are estimated can suggest improvements in how learning directions are estimated, within the framework developed in the paper.
icml-2020-from-importance-sampling-to-do.tldr: Deriving policy gradients from off-policy value estimators yields a flexible doubly robust estimator and new variance-reduction opportunities.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify a particular object through a small relational program. The input is a symbolic representation of an image and a target object. The desired program uses the object’s attributes and its relationships to other objects to distinguish it uniquely within the scene.

The authors combine a policy neural network with enumerative search in a neurosymbolic synthesis algorithm. A program interpreter supplies immediate feedback about the consequences of the policy’s decisions. The policy also accounts for uncertainty in the symbolic image representation, so the program-generation process incorporates both executable reasoning and uncertainty about the scene it describes.

Experiments on challenging benchmarks derived from CLEVR show significant improvements over several baselines. The approach matters because generating a reference is treated as constructing an executable object-selection procedure. Interpreter feedback connects generation decisions to their effects on the represented scene, while search and the neural policy work together to find programs that identify the intended target.
icml-2020-generating-programmatic-referr.tldr: A neural policy, program interpreter, and enumerative search jointly generate relational programs that uniquely identify objects in symbolic scenes.

paragraphs: Training attention-based models can be unstable, with learning-rate warmup used to prevent divergence. As Transformers grow deeper and more expensive, understanding the source of that instability becomes increasingly useful. This paper investigates optimization problems in encoder-decoder Transformers and empirically validates its account of their source.

The authors then propose a weight-initialization scheme supported by theoretical reasoning. It enables training without learning-rate warmup or layer normalization. The intervention acts at the beginning of optimization, making the initial parameter configuration a central part of the solution to the training difficulties examined in the study.

On public machine translation benchmarks, the method achieves leading accuracy and supports models with 200 layers in both the encoder and decoder, totaling more than 1,000 attention and multilayer-perceptron blocks. These results demonstrate that the proposed initialization can support very deep Transformer training in the evaluated setting. The contribution combines an explanation of optimization behavior with a concrete initialization method and evidence of successful large-depth training.
icml-2020-improving-transformer-optimiza.tldr: A theoretically motivated initialization scheme enables very deep encoder-decoder Transformers to train without warmup or layer normalization.

paragraphs: Connections between wide neural networks and Gaussian processes offer mathematical ways to study network predictions and training. This paper extends that theory to networks containing attention layers. A central finding is that attention’s structure matters: single-head attention produces non-Gaussian behavior, while multi-head attention approaches Gaussian-process behavior as the number of heads grows without bound.

The authors also examine how positional encodings and layer normalization affect these models. They propose attention modifications that improve results for both finite networks and their infinite-width counterparts. This connects the limiting theory to architectural choices that also matter in networks with finite computational resources.

Empirical evaluation of attention kernels yields a moderate CIFAR-10 improvement over the previous best results within the stated category of Gaussian processes without trainable kernels or advanced preprocessing. The work also extends the Neural Tangents library to support variable-length sequences for NNGP and NTK models, including attention-based versions, and demonstrates that capability on IMDb reviews.
icml-2020-infinite-attention-nngp-and-nt.tldr: Multi-head attention has a Gaussian-process limit as head count grows, enabling theoretical analysis and practical attention-kernel models.

paragraphs: InstaHide addresses training a shared neural network across entities that wish to protect their private images. The proposed transformation mixes each image with other images and then applies a random mask at the pixel level. The resulting images can enter standard deep learning and federated learning pipelines without additional infrastructure.

The paper reports only a minor effect on test accuracy and studies mixing with images from a large public dataset as a way to improve security. Its experiments demonstrate protection against the known attacks evaluated while preserving model accuracy. A theoretical analysis also connects successful privacy attacks to solving a difficult computational problem.

The authors separately show that Mixup alone is insecure by constructing efficient attacks, distinguishing that component from the full InstaHide procedure. They also release a challenge dataset to support development of further attacks. The stated evidence combines practical attack evaluations and computational analysis; the empirical protection described concerns the tested attacks rather than establishing immunity to every possible attack.
icml-2020-instahide-instance-hiding-sche.tldr: InstaHide combines image mixing and random pixel masks to protect training images, with reported accuracy preservation and resistance to evaluated attacks.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether epidemic cascades can reveal the weighted connections of two underlying graphs when observations come from a mixture of them. Recovering both graphs requires distinguishing the structures contributing to the observed spreading behavior. The main setting is a balanced mixture of two undirected graphs.

For edge-separated graphs, the authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for polynomial-time recovery. Within that setting, the stated conditions require connected graphs with at least three edges. When these conditions hold, their algorithm efficiently learns both sets of edge weights, using a number of samples that is optimal up to logarithmic factors.

The paper also develops complementary algorithms for directed-graph mixtures with out-degree at least three and for undirected mixtures whose proportions are unbalanced or unknown. These algorithms likewise have sample-optimal guarantees up to logarithmic factors. The contribution identifies when recovery is computationally possible in the specified graph setting and supplies methods with near-optimal data requirements for several related mixture models.
icml-2020-learning-mixtures-of-graphs-fr.tldr: The paper characterizes efficient recoverability of edge-separated graph mixtures from epidemic cascades and provides near-sample-optimal algorithms.

paragraphs: Multiple-object tracking requires linking detections across time into consistent object trajectories. This paper extends the disjoint paths problem with lifted edges that express preferences about path connectivity. These additional connections provide a mathematical way to include interactions between detections that are far apart in time.

The resulting lifted disjoint paths problem is NP-hard, as shown through reductions from integer multicommodity flow and 3-SAT. To make optimization practical, the authors develop classes of linear inequalities that strengthen a linear-programming relaxation. Efficient cutting-plane algorithms identify relevant inequalities, allowing the optimization procedure to use these constraints effectively.

In tracking, lifted edges help maintain identities and re-identify people, addressing decisions that depend on more than nearby frames. The proposed tracker obtains assignments that are nearly optimal relative to its input detections. The authors report leading performance on all three main MOT challenge benchmarks, with significant gains over prior methods. This ties the richer connectivity model and its optimization machinery to improved tracking outcomes.
icml-2020-lifted-disjoint-paths-with-app.tldr: Lifted edges model long-range tracking relationships, while strong relaxations and cutting planes make the resulting hard optimization problem practical.

paragraphs: Research on differentiable games often proposes algorithms and establishes how quickly they can converge. This paper studies the complementary question of fundamental iteration complexity: lower bounds that help describe limits on achievable convergence. Its focus is linear convergence, meaning geometric progress rather than an error that decreases by a fixed amount.

The authors formulate saddle-point and min-max problems as two-player games, then adapt tools from single-objective convex optimization to obtain lower bounds for convex-concave games. They also derive a linear lower bound for games with multiple players by analyzing spectral properties of the update operator, connecting convergence limits to the structure of the learning updates.

From this analysis, the paper proposes a new condition number for differentiable games. It captures the possibility of linear convergence even when strong convexity or strong concavity is absent from the variables. This matters because a measure of conditioning should reflect the convergence behavior that games can actually exhibit, including behavior that earlier definitions fail to capture.
icml-2020-linear-lower-bounds-and-condit.tldr: New convergence lower bounds motivate a game condition number that captures possible linear rates without strong convexity or concavity.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic approach to meta-learning in which model parameters are latent variables. With limited training examples, the method learns a distribution over those parameters rather than committing to one fixed setting. It uses an empirical Bayes model and a variational-autoencoder approach to learn a data-conditioned prior.

The central design shares one amortized inference network between the conditional prior and the variational posterior. Their information differs: the prior uses labeled support examples, while the posterior can also use labeled query examples. Sharing the inference mechanism connects these distributions while preserving the distinction between the data available to each.

The authors show that a Monte Carlo approximation used in earlier work causes the conditional prior to collapse to a single point, eliminating parameter uncertainty. Their variational approach prevents that collapse and retains a distribution over possible parameters. Experiments on miniImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC100 demonstrate advantages over previous work, supporting uncertainty preservation as a useful component of this meta-learning framework.
icml-2020-meta-learning-with-shared-amor.tldr: Shared variational inference preserves uncertainty over meta-learned model parameters by preventing the conditional prior from collapsing to a point.

paragraphs: This paper proposes policy-gradient methods for model-free reinforcement learning that combine momentum with variance reduction. The aim is to make learning efficient without requiring large batches of trajectories. The main methods use adaptive learning rates and reuse information through a new momentum-based variance-reduction technique.

Two versions combine that technique with different ingredients. IS-MBPG uses importance sampling, while HA-MBPG uses Hessian information. The authors prove that both reach the stated best-known sample complexity of O(ε⁻³) for finding an ε-stationary point of the nonconcave performance objective, using only one trajectory per iteration. The guarantee targets approximate stationarity, rather than a globally optimal policy.

A further method, IS-MBPG*, removes adaptive learning rates while retaining the same sample-complexity order and avoiding large batches. Experiments on four benchmark tasks demonstrate the algorithms’ effectiveness. Together, the results show that the stated sample-efficiency bound can be achieved with small per-iteration data requirements through several related momentum-based designs, including a non-adaptive variant.
icml-2020-momentum-based-policy-gradient.tldr: Momentum-based policy-gradient methods achieve the stated best-known stationarity sample complexity without large trajectory batches.

paragraphs: Face-recognition training often encourages features to lie close to their corresponding identity centers using margin-based losses. This paper argues that strong performance under such comparison objectives does not explicitly encourage the general embeddings needed for open-set recognition. The goal is therefore to improve how learned face representations generalize beyond the training identities.

The authors analyze margin-based softmax loss through a probabilistic perspective and propose two principles for designing margin losses: monotonic decrease and a margin probability penalty. They also frame open-set recognition as information transmission, arguing that cleaner information supports better generalization. A proposed autoencoder architecture, Linear-Auto-TS-Encoder, or LATSE, is used to substantiate that view.

Experiments across several benchmarks show improved generalization of face embeddings with LATSE. The paper reports performance above 99% on the MegaFace test for a single model trained using an open training dataset. The findings connect probabilistic loss design and information-focused representation learning to the observed recognition improvements, with the reported numerical result tied to that specific evaluation setting.
icml-2020-more-information-supervised-pr.tldr: A probabilistic loss perspective and the LATSE autoencoder improve face-embedding generalization for open-set recognition.

paragraphs: This paper builds long-term memory into a neural network by distributing memory cells alongside computation. Its architecture uses a multigrid organization, with hierarchical spatial structure and convolutional parameterization. The design aims to provide large memory capacity while allowing memory access to emerge through the network’s learned internal behavior.

Multigrid connectivity supplies short routes between internal locations, helping a convolutional network approximate fully connected behavior efficiently. With memory added, the network learns data-dependent reading and writing at particular locations. The authors observe coherent memory subsystems emerging from this organization, without requiring an external memory bank controlled by a separately crafted attention mechanism.

On exploration and mapping tasks, the network self-organizes and retains information over trajectories lasting thousands of time steps. It also performs well on sorting, associative recall, and question answering, which do not depend on spatial geometry. These results support the usefulness of the memory architecture beyond spatial tasks: a spatially organized network can learn memory operations for several kinds of information processing.
icml-2020-multigrid-neural-memory-0c9de8.tldr: A multigrid network learns internal memory access and retains information across long trajectories and nonspatial reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: A control policy is usually trained for one agent’s body, with a particular number of sensors and actuators. This paper investigates whether one policy can control agents with different skeletal structures, even when their state and action spaces have different dimensions. Its solution expresses control through repeated local modules.

Shared Modular Policies assign an identical neural-network module to each actuator. Each module controls its own actuator using local sensory information, while messages exchanged among modules carry information across the body. This arrangement combines local control with a communication mechanism capable of supporting coordination between distant parts of an agent.

The authors demonstrate locomotion for several planar morphologies, including monopod hoppers, quadrupeds, and bipeds, and transfer to variants absent from training. They observe diverse locomotion styles and centralized coordination emerging through messages between decentralized modules, driven solely by the reinforcement-learning objective. The results show that one shared modular policy can handle the evaluated range of bodies without separately training and manually tuning a policy for each morphology.
icml-2020-one-policy-to-control-them-all.tldr: Identical actuator-level controllers communicate to form one shared policy that controls multiple body shapes and generalizes to unseen variants.

paragraphs: Zero-shot coordination asks whether an agent can cooperate with a partner it has never encountered during training. Standard self-play trains agents through repeated interaction with themselves. This can create highly specialized conventions that work within training partnerships but fail to transfer to independently trained agents or human partners.

The paper introduces other-play, an algorithm that enhances self-play by seeking more robust strategies. The authors characterize the method both theoretically and experimentally. The central objective is to make learned cooperation useful beyond the particular partners and conventions established during training, addressing the gap between successful self-play and successful interaction with someone new.

Experiments use the cooperative card game Hanabi. Other-play agents achieve higher scores than self-play agents when paired with independently trained partners and when paired with humans. These results demonstrate an advantage in the studied coordination setting and make partner compatibility an explicit criterion for evaluating learning. They also show why performance with familiar training partners alone does not establish an agent’s ability to cooperate with unfamiliar ones.
icml-2020-other-play-for-zero-shot-coord.tldr: Other-play learns more robust cooperative strategies and improves Hanabi coordination with independently trained agents and humans.

paragraphs: Many real-world time series contain measurements taken at uneven intervals, with different variables recorded at different times. Such asynchronous observations can be difficult to accommodate in existing neural architectures. This paper introduces SeFT, a classification method designed for irregularly sampled time series with unaligned measurements, particularly in healthcare settings.

SeFT builds on differentiable set-function learning, with scalability and data efficiency as design priorities. Its computation is highly parallelizable and has a favorable memory footprint. These properties make it suitable for large datasets, long observation sequences, and online monitoring. The approach also allows individual observations’ contributions to a classification outcome to be quantified.

Comparisons across multiple healthcare time-series datasets show competitive predictive performance together with significantly reduced runtime. The result is a practical combination of classification quality and computational efficiency in the evaluated settings. Its per-observation contribution estimates additionally provide a way to examine which recorded measurements influence a decision, complementing the system’s focus on handling irregular data efficiently.
icml-2020-set-functions-for-time-series-.tldr: SeFT uses differentiable set functions to classify irregular time series competitively while significantly reducing runtime.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning combines training across devices or locations whose datasets may have different distributions. This paper studies one common form of that mismatch: unequal distributions of labels across participants. Its experimental investigation examines how this label skew affects deep-network training across applications, architectures, datasets, and decentralized learning algorithms.

The study finds significant accuracy losses across the examined settings and identifies skew severity as an important determinant of difficulty. Networks using batch normalization are particularly affected. These findings connect the decentralized data distribution to both training-system behavior and a specific architectural choice, showing that the same degree of coordination may not suit every partitioning of data.

The authors introduce SkewScout, which adapts communication frequency according to accuracy loss induced by differences between data partitions. They also show that replacing batch normalization with group normalization can recover much of the lost accuracy. The proposed responses therefore operate at two levels: communication adapts to observed consequences of skew, while the normalization choice addresses a particularly vulnerable part of the model.
icml-2020-the-non-iid-data-quagmire-of-d.tldr: Label skew harms decentralized learning, motivating adaptive communication through SkewScout and accuracy recovery through group normalization.

paragraphs: Broad language benchmarks help assess whether models work across different tasks, but many such evaluations concentrate on English. XTREME addresses the need to evaluate multilingual representations across both task types and languages. It covers 40 languages and nine tasks, focusing on how well linguistic knowledge transfers across languages.

The evaluation reveals a substantial gap between strong English performance and cross-lingual transfer performance. Although models evaluated in English reach human performance on many tasks, transferred models remain considerably weaker, especially on syntactic tasks and sentence retrieval. Results also vary widely across languages, making language coverage an important part of the assessment.

The benchmark’s contribution is a shared framework for examining these differences across a diverse collection of settings. Its findings show that success on English tasks does not establish equally strong multilingual transfer. By bringing multiple tasks and languages into one evaluation, XTREME helps expose where transfer remains difficult and supports research aimed at spreading linguistic knowledge more effectively across languages.
icml-2020-xtreme-a-massively-multilingua.tldr: XTREME evaluates cross-lingual transfer across 40 languages and nine tasks, revealing substantial performance gaps and variation between languages.
